items.name: Lead
items.desc: Often leaches from old pipes and solder. Toxic even at low doses, and particularly dangerous for children's neurological development.

items.name: Arsenic
items.desc: Naturally present in some rocks, it can contaminate well water. It is a known carcinogen with serious long-term health effects.

items.name: Mercury
items.desc: A highly toxic heavy metal, often from industrial discharges or natural processes. Can cause serious damage to the nervous system and kidneys.

items.name: Iron and manganese
items.desc: Very common in wells. Although of little danger to health, they cause stubborn stains (rust, black), cloudy water and an unpleasant metallic taste.

items.name: Copper
items.desc: Usually comes from the corrosion of copper pipes. Can cause gastrointestinal problems and damage the liver at high doses.

items.name: Barium
items.desc: A natural element sometimes found in groundwater. Prolonged exposure can lead to cardiovascular problems and higher blood pressure.

items.name: Aluminum
items.desc: Sometimes present after municipal treatment. Although mostly removed, traces can remain.

items.name: Zinc
items.desc: Often comes from the corrosion of galvanized pipes. It mainly affects the appearance and taste of water.

items.name: Cadmium
items.desc: Gets in through the corrosion of galvanized pipes or industrial discharges. It builds up in the body and is very toxic to the kidneys.

items.name: Chromium (total and chromium VI)
items.desc: Comes from industrial discharges (metallurgy, tanneries). Hexavalent chromium (VI) is highly carcinogenic.

items.name: Selenium
items.desc: A natural element or from mining/agricultural discharges. Useful in traces, but toxic to the nervous system and circulation at high doses.

items.name: Strontium
items.desc: A natural mineral. At high concentrations, it can build up in bones and interfere with bone development, especially in children.

items.name: Antimony
items.desc: Used in alloys and flame retardants. Prolonged exposure can affect the heart and the gastrointestinal tract.

items.name: E. coli and fecal coliforms
items.desc: Indicate recent fecal contamination. They cause severe gastrointestinal illness and require immediate action (boiling, UV treatment).

items.name: Total coliforms
items.desc: Bacteria naturally present in the environment. Their presence indicates that the system is vulnerable to pathogens.

items.name: Giardia and Cryptosporidium
items.desc: Chlorine-resistant microscopic parasites, often found in surface water. They cause serious intestinal illness.

items.name: Iron and sulphur bacteria
items.desc: Non-pathogenic bacteria that create slimy sludge in plumbing and can produce foul odours.

items.name: Cyanobacteria (blue-green algae)
items.desc: They thrive in lakes and rivers in summer and produce toxins that are dangerous for the liver and the nervous system.

items.name: Enteric viruses
items.desc: Include viruses such as hepatitis A and norovirus. Extremely small, they require disinfection or ultra-fine filtration.

items.name: Chlorine and chloramines
items.desc: Used by municipalities to disinfect water. They can give water an unpleasant taste and smell, and dry out skin and hair.

items.name: Trihalomethanes (THMs)
items.desc: Carcinogenic by-products formed when chlorine reacts with organic matter.

items.name: Haloacetic acids (HAAs)
items.desc: Another class of chlorination by-products. Toxic to the liver and kidneys and potentially carcinogenic.

items.name: Chlorite and chlorate
items.desc: By-products formed when chlorine dioxide is used as a disinfectant.

items.name: Bromate
items.desc: A carcinogenic by-product generated when water is disinfected with ozone.

items.name: N-Nitrosodimethylamine (NDMA)
items.desc: Forms during water treatment (often with chloramines). Highly carcinogenic.

items.name: PFAS ("forever chemicals")
items.desc: Perfluoroalkyl substances used in many industrial products. They build up in the environment and the body, causing various cancers.

items.name: Benzene, toluene, ethylbenzene, xylenes (BTEX)
items.desc: Industrial solvents and petroleum components, often linked to leaking underground tanks. Neurotoxic and carcinogenic.

items.name: Tetrachloroethylene and trichloroethylene
items.desc: Dry-cleaning and degreasing solvents. Common groundwater contaminants and probable carcinogens.

items.name: 1,4-Dioxane
items.desc: An industrial stabilizing solvent, extremely mobile in groundwater. A potential carcinogen.

items.name: Vinyl chloride
items.desc: A component of PVC plastics that can leach from old pipes. Highly carcinogenic.

items.name: Formaldehyde
items.desc: An industrial product or oxidation by-product. Highly irritating and carcinogenic.

items.name: Cyanide
items.desc: Mainly from industrial discharges (mining, metallurgy). Extremely toxic in the short term.

items.name: Asbestos
items.desc: Leached by the erosion of old asbestos-cement water mains. Ingestion is linked to polyps and digestive cancers.

items.name: Atrazine and glyphosate
items.desc: Widely used agricultural herbicides carried by runoff. Potential endocrine disruptors.

items.name: 2,4-D, MCPA, dicamba
items.desc: Common selective herbicides. Long-term exposure can damage the liver and kidneys.

items.name: Chlorpyrifos, malathion, dimethoate
items.desc: Neurotoxic organophosphate insecticides that can contaminate wells in farming areas.

items.name: Pentachlorophenol
items.desc: A historical fungicide used to treat wood (utility poles). Highly toxic and carcinogenic.

items.name: Diquat
items.desc: An aquatic herbicide used to control algae. Can cause eye and kidney damage.

items.name: Scale (water hardness)
items.desc: Made of calcium and magnesium. It poses no health risk, but scales up water heaters, destroys appliances and clogs pipes.

items.name: Nitrates and nitrites
items.desc: Often come from agricultural fertilizers or faulty septic tanks. Very dangerous for infants (blue baby syndrome).

items.name: Hydrogen sulphide (H2S)
items.desc: A dissolved gas that gives water a strong rotten egg smell. Corrosive to plumbing.

items.name: Sodium
items.desc: Often added by traditional salt-based water softeners or naturally present. Something to watch for people on a low-sodium diet.

items.name: Sulphates
items.desc: Give water a bitter taste and can have a temporary laxative effect on people who are not used to them.

items.name: Uranium and radon
items.desc: Radioactive elements naturally present in Canadian bedrock (the Canadian Shield). They carry long-term risks of cancer or kidney damage.

items.name: Radium-226 and radium-228
items.desc: Radioactive isotopes from the decay of uranium/thorium. They increase the risk of bone cancer.

items.name: Lead-210
items.desc: An element of the radioactive decay chain, toxic through its radiological emissions.

micro.recommandation: MAC of none detectable per 100 mL in water leaving a treatment plant and in non-disinfected groundwater leaving the well
micro.sources: Human and animal feces; naturally present in water, soil and vegetation
micro.sante: Total coliforms are not used as indicators of potential health effects from pathogenic micro-organisms; they are used as a tool to determine the effectiveness of the water treatment system and to indicate changes in water quality in the distribution system.

E. coli is an indicator of fecal contamination used as a tool to verify drinking water quality. Its detection indicates recent fecal contamination and that micro-organisms capable of causing gastrointestinal illness may also be present. Pathogens in human and animal feces pose the greatest immediate danger to public health.

micro.contaminant: Enteric protozoa: Giardia and Cryptosporidium (2019) Water Talk - Enteric protozoa (Giardia and Cryptosporidium) in drinking water
micro.recommandation: Treatment goal: removal and/or inactivation of at least 3 log of cysts and oocysts
micro.sante: Giardia and Cryptosporidium are generally associated with gastrointestinal illness (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea). Less common health effects vary. Giardia infections can include long-lasting gastrointestinal upset, malaise and malabsorption. In immunodeficient individuals, Cryptosporidium infections can have effects outside the gastrointestinal tract, including in the lungs, middle ear and pancreas.

micro.recommandation: Treatment limits for water from individual filters or units: conventional or direct filtration: ≤ 0.3 NTU; slow sand or diatomaceous earth filtration: ≤ 1.0 NTU; membrane filtration: ≤ 0.1 NTU
micro.sources: Naturally occurring particles: inorganic matter (clay, silt, metal precipitates); organic matter (decomposed plant and animal debris, micro-organisms)
micro.sante: Particles can harbour micro-organisms, shielding them from disinfection, and trap heavy metals and biocides; high or changing turbidity in filtered water can indicate a problem in the treatment process and a possible increased risk of pathogens in the treated water.

micro.contaminant: Enteric viruses (2019) Water Talk - Enteric viruses in drinking water
micro.recommandation: Treatment goal: reduction (removal or inactivation) of at least 4 log
micro.sante: Generally associated with gastrointestinal illness (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea); less common health effects can include respiratory symptoms, central nervous system infections, liver infections and muscular syndromes.
